name: Blush for men

lead: Blush is a cosmetic that adds colour to the cheeks, in powder, cream, liquid or gel form. Men using it aim for the look of a healthy flush, warmth in pale or tired-looking skin, or a little definition around the cheekbones.

The effect lasts as long as the product is worn. Wikipedia notes that blush has long been used to accentuate bone structure, and that men used rouge in ancient Egypt, Greece, Rome and 16th-century Europe.

paras: Typically a small amount of a cream or tint is dabbed onto the apples or upper cheekbones and blended so it reads as natural skin colour; shades close to a natural flush are chosen. It is usually applied after skincare and base, alongside concealer or tinted moisturiser.

Possible irritation or allergic reaction to ingredients and clogged pores with heavy products; patch testing and removal at night are standard cosmetic guidance. Historical rouges based on red lead and cinnabar were toxic, which modern cosmetics avoid.[1]

angle.text: Blush adds colour to the cheeks, which makes skin look warmer and healthier. Placed along the cheekbones it can add definition. The result lasts while the product is worn.

lead: Blush, also called blusher or rouge, is a cosmetic that colours the cheeks and comes as a pressed or loose powder, a cream, a liquid or a gel.[1] For men, it is a grooming tool for adding a natural flush to skin that looks pale, tired or flat.

Applied on the cheekbones, blush can also accentuate bone structure.[1] Historically, men and women used rouge in several cultures: Egyptians mixed fat with red ochre, Greeks used mulberries and beet juice, and 16th-century European men wore white powder with heavy rouge.[1]
No clinical research examines male blush use specifically; its effect is cosmetic and temporary.

paras: Traditional rouge was a red, talc-based powder coloured with safflower petals or carmine; modern products include pressed powder, lipstick-like creams, liquids and gels.[1]

Rouge appears in ancient Egypt, Shang-dynasty China (safflower leaf juice), Greece and Rome. Roman rouge made from red lead and cinnabar is said to have been toxic.[1] Men and women of 16th-century Europe wore heavy rouge over white face powder.[1]

In grooming discussions, male blush is presented as a way to reproduce a healthy flush or to add warmth to winter-pale skin. This sits alongside concealer, tinted moisturiser and brow products as part of a light make-up routine.
No studies found. Related research on natural blushing treats it as a social signal, not as a cosmetic effect.[1]
